The Greeks set their
greatest stories here.
Jason sailed here for the Golden Fleece. Prometheus was chained to these peaks. Georgians have a few legends of their own.
Jason and the Argonauts sailed to Colchis — western Georgia — for a ram's fleece of gold. One theory traces the myth to Svan villagers who laid sheepskins in mountain streams to catch gold dust.

Greek myth chained Prometheus to a peak in the Caucasus for giving fire to humans; Georgian tradition places him on Kazbek. Georgians have their own fire-thief hero, Amirani, chained in a mountain cave.
When God divided the earth, the Georgians arrived late — they had been feasting and toasting Him. Charmed, God gave them the land He had been keeping for Himself.
St Nino walked into Georgia carrying a cross of grapevines tied with her own hair. Wine and faith have been bound together here ever since.
სტუმარი ღვთისაა · The guest is from God
In Georgia, a guest is a gift from God. Expect to be fed until you surrender, toasted by strangers, and sent home with a bottle of somebody's grandfather's wine.
A Georgian feast is led by a tamada, the toastmaster, through toasts to peace, to ancestors, to friendship and to you. It can last all night. Pace yourself.
Georgian polyphonic singing is UNESCO-listed — and in 1977 the song Chakrulo was sent into deep space on the Voyager Golden Record.
Cheese bread with an egg on top. Soup dumplings you eat by hand, never with a fork. Walnuts, pomegranate, tarragon. You will not leave hungry.

History of Georgia · Million First Steps
The history of Georgia in one scroll: Dmanisi's 1.8-million-year-old humans, 8,000 years of wine, Colchis and the Golden Fleece, St Nino, David the Builder, King Tamar and today.

Few countries can tell the human story from its very first chapter. Georgia can: the first humans outside Africa, the first wine, one of the first Christian kingdoms, an alphabet all its own — and a hospitality that survived everything.
Empires came from every direction — Persian, Roman, Arab, Byzantine, Mongol, Ottoman, Russian. Georgians kept their language, their faith, their songs and their wine. Walk through it with us.

On a basalt promontory at Dmanisi, south of Tbilisi, archaeologists have found the remains of the earliest humans known outside Africa — five skulls and many more bones, dated to roughly 1.85–1.77 million years ago.

Skull 5, published in 2013, is the most complete early human skull of its age ever found. These people were small, tool-making early Homo — and they changed what scientists thought about when, and how, humans first left Africa.
Someone buries a jar of wine

At the Neolithic villages of Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora, about 50 km south of Tbilisi, pottery jars still carry the chemical signature of grape wine. Published in 2017, they are the earliest known evidence of grape winemaking anywhere on Earth.
The method Georgians still use — fermenting and ageing wine in egg-shaped clay qvevri buried in the ground — was inscribed by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2013.

Western Georgia was Colchis, a land so rich in gold that the Greeks set one of their greatest myths there: Jason and the Argonauts sailing east to steal the Golden Fleece from King Aeëtes, helped by his daughter Medea.
The gold was real. Excavations at Vani have uncovered extraordinary Colchian jewellery, and the ancient geographer Strabo described mountain people catching gold dust from rivers in fleeces.

In the east rose the kingdom the Greeks and Romans called Iberia — Kartli to Georgians — with its capital at Mtskheta, where two rivers meet. Medieval chronicles credit its first king, Pharnavaz, with uniting the land.
For centuries Iberia balanced between Rome and Persia, trading along routes that would later be called the Silk Road.

According to tradition, a young woman named Nino came from Cappadocia carrying a cross made of grapevine branches, bound with her own hair. She converted Queen Nana and King Mirian III, and in the early 4th century Kartli became one of the first kingdoms in the world to adopt Christianity as its state religion.
The vine cross of St Nino is still the symbol of the Georgian Church. Her resting place is at Bodbe, above the vineyards of Kakheti.

Georgian has an alphabet entirely its own — rounded, curling letters you will see nowhere else on Earth. The oldest securely dated inscriptions are from the 5th century — including those at Bolnisi Sioni, dated 493–494.
Three scripts grew from it: Asomtavruli, Nuskhuri and today's flowing Mkhedruli. In 2016 UNESCO inscribed the living culture of all three writing systems as Intangible Cultural Heritage.
A playful approximation — Georgian has sounds English doesn't, and vice versa. (მოგზაური means "traveller".)
Legend says King Vakhtang Gorgasali was hunting when a pheasant his falcon had caught fell into a hot spring. He ordered a city built on the spot and named it Tbilisi — from tbili, warm.
The sulphur springs still flow beneath the brick domes of the Abanotubani bath quarter.

King David IV inherited a weak, half-occupied kingdom and rebuilt it. On 12 August 1121, at Didgori, his army defeated a much larger Seljuk coalition; the next year he took back Tbilisi and made it his capital.
He founded Gelati Monastery and its academy in 1106 — and asked to be buried beneath its gate, so that everyone who entered would walk over him.
The golden age of King Tamar

His great-granddaughter Tamar ruled as mepe — king, not queen — over Georgia's golden age, when its influence stretched across the Caucasus. The cliff city of Vardzia flourished under her, and her portrait is still on its church wall.
Shota Rustaveli dedicated his epic, The Knight in the Panther's Skin, to her. Georgians still quote it, and many brides were once given a copy as part of their dowry.
Invasions, and a culture that endured

Mongol armies arrived in the 1220s; Timur invaded repeatedly between 1386 and 1403. The united kingdom eventually broke into smaller kingdoms and principalities, contested by Persian and Ottoman empires.

In the high valleys of Svaneti, families built stone defensive towers — most between the 9th and 12th centuries — and kept icons, manuscripts and treasures safe through it all. Upper Svaneti is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

In 1783 King Erekle II of Kartli-Kakheti signed the Treaty of Georgievsk, placing his kingdom under Russian protection. In 1801 the Russian Empire annexed it, and in the decades after, the rest of Georgia.

The 19th century brought a cultural revival: writers like Ilia Chavchavadze — now remembered as the father of the modern nation — and, at Tsinandali, Alexander Chavchavadze's estate, where European-style wine met Georgian tradition.
A republic, and a long Soviet century
On 26 May 1918 Georgia declared independence as the Democratic Republic of Georgia. In 1921 the Red Army invaded, and Georgia spent the next seventy years inside the Soviet Union.
In 1977 a Georgian folk song, Chakrulo, was chosen for the Golden Record carried into deep space by the Voyager probes — Georgian polyphony is now travelling beyond the solar system.
On 9 April 1991 Georgia restored its independence. Today it welcomes travellers from all over the world — citizens of around 95 countries can visit without a visa, many for up to a year.
And it still keeps the old rule: a guest is a gift from God. The million-and-first step through this land could be yours.

Founded in the 5th century over hot springs, Tbilisi piles churches, mosques, a synagogue and Art Nouveau mansions onto the cliffs of the Mtkvari. By day: markets, museums and bakeries. By night: natural-wine bars and dinners that run past midnight.

Three hours up the Georgian Military Road, Stepantsminda sits beneath Mount Kazbek, the dormant volcano where Greek myth chained Prometheus. Above it all, the lonely Gergeti Trinity Church — the image that probably made you look up Georgia in the first place.

Cut off for centuries, Svaneti kept its own language, its own laws and hundreds of defensive towers. Upper Svaneti is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and Ushguli — at around 2,100 metres — is one of the highest continuously inhabited villages in Europe.

Most of Georgia's wine comes from this broad valley under the snowy wall of the Greater Caucasus. Families still ferment grapes in clay qvevri, monks still make wine at Alaverdi, and every meal can turn into a supra.

The south-west is volcanic highland and deep canyons: Vardzia's cave city, the restored citadel of Rabati, the spa town of Borjomi with its famous mineral springs, and one of the largest national parks in the Caucasus.

Green, humid and full of legends: Kutaisi and its UNESCO-listed Gelati Monastery, dinosaur footprints at Sataplia, the underground halls of Prometheus Cave and the emerald canyons of Martvili and Okatse.
Batumi's seafront and Botanical Garden, the Roman fort at Gonio and, a few minutes inland, the Colchic rainforest of Mtirala National Park — part of a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2021.

Reachable only over the Abano pass, and only for a few months a year, Tusheti is Georgia at its wildest: tower villages like Dartlo, flocks moving between pastures, and night skies with no light pollution at all.

The quiet uplands south of Tbilisi hold two of the world's great archaeological stories: the 1.8-million-year-old hominins of Dmanisi, and the Neolithic villages where the earliest known grape wine was made, around 6000 BC.

Million First Steps is a small, family-run Georgian travel company. We plan every journey ourselves, and we treat every traveller as a guest at our own table.

Because the first steps
were taken here.
About 1.8 million years ago, early humans walked out of Africa and into the hills of what is now Georgia. Their bones, found at Dmanisi, are the oldest human fossils ever discovered outside Africa.

Since then, Georgia has been crossed by traders on the Silk Road, Greek sailors chasing a golden fleece, saints, poets and armies — a million footsteps, give or take. We think yours should be the next one. The million-and-first.

One of us has spent a lifetime on Georgia's roads and knows which village bakery is still warm at dawn. The other grew up being dragged along — and now can't stop showing the country off to anyone who will listen.
Knows the roads, the winemakers and the stories behind every church. Has an opinion about the best khinkali in every valley — and he's usually right.

Practical advice for visiting Georgia: visas, money, language, the best time to visit each region, etiquette and frequently asked questions.
Visas, money, seasons, manners at the table — the practical side of a trip to Georgia, from people who live here.

Citizens of around 95 countries — including the EU, UK, USA, Canada and Australia — can visit visa-free, most for up to a year. Others can apply online through Georgia's official e-visa portal. Always check the Ministry of Foreign Affairs website before you travel.
The currency is the Georgian lari (GEL, ₾). Cards work almost everywhere in cities; carry some cash for villages, markets and the mountains. ATMs are easy to find.
Georgian, with its own alphabet. Many older people speak Russian and more and more young people speak English. Gamarjoba = hello, madloba = thank you, gaumarjos = cheers!
Georgia Standard Time, GMT+4 all year round — no daylight saving.
220 V, 50 Hz, with European two-pin plugs (types C and F).
International airports at Tbilisi (TBS), Kutaisi (KUT) and Batumi (BUS). We meet every guest at arrivals.
Georgia is widely regarded as a safe, welcoming country. Mountain weather changes fast and roads wind — which is why we drive. Travel insurance is required on all our journeys.
Dial 112 for police, ambulance or fire. Our team is reachable 24/7 throughout your trip.

There's no bad month —
only different Georgias.
Spring is green and full of flowers, summer opens the high mountains, autumn brings the harvest, and winter means skiing and quiet, snowy monasteries.

Georgians forgive almost anything from a guest. But these will win you friends.
Cover shoulders and knees; women usually cover their hair. Scarves and wraps are often available at the door.
Wait for the tamada's toast before you drink wine. Never toast with beer — that is traditionally reserved for enemies.
Eat with your hands: hold the knot, bite, sip the broth, then eat the rest. Leave the knot on your plate — it's how people count.
Many restaurants add a 10% service charge; check the bill. Otherwise, rounding up is appreciated, never expected.

Yes. Every journey is private, so we can add a day in the mountains, swap a museum for a winery or combine two tours. The published itineraries are starting points.
What's the difference between the tiers?

The route and experiences are the same. Wanderer uses guesthouses and simpler cars, Explorer boutique hotels and a separate guide and driver, Golden Fleece the best hotels, all meals and a senior expert guide. See the comparison on the Tours page.
Do you cater for vegetarians and allergies?
Easily. Georgian cooking is full of vegetarian and vegan dishes — lobio beans, walnut pkhali, aubergine rolls — partly thanks to the Orthodox fasting tradition. Tell us about allergies when you book.
How far ahead should I book?
Two to four months ahead for summer and the September–October harvest; a few weeks is often enough at other times. Tusheti and the best Golden Fleece hotels fill up first.
Is Georgia suitable for children and older travellers?
Very. Georgians adore children, and every itinerary can slow down. Tell us who's coming and we'll pace the days accordingly.

How Million First Steps handles your personal data. No cookies, no tracking.
Short version: this website doesn't track you. We only receive the details you choose to send us, and we use them only to plan your trip.
Million First Steps, Tbilisi, Georgia — “we”, “us”. Contact: hello@millionfirststeps.ge.
No cookies, no analytics, no advertising trackers. We don't use Google Analytics, Facebook pixels or similar tools.
Fonts and scripts are hosted on this website. Your browser does not contact Google Fonts or any other third-party content service when you visit.
Your preferences stay on your device. If you choose a currency or travel style, your browser remembers it in local storage. It never leaves your device and you can clear it at any time.
Our web host may keep standard server logs (such as IP address and pages requested) for security and to keep the site running.
When you send us a request

If you use our form or write to us, we receive what you give us: typically your name, email address, phone number, country, travel dates, party size and any notes (such as dietary or mobility needs). The form opens your own email program, so your request is sent by you, from your email account, directly to us.

We use these details only to reply to you, to plan and operate your journey, and — once you book — to meet our legal and accounting obligations. To run your trip we share only what's needed with the hotels, drivers and guides who host you. We never sell your data or use it for advertising.
Requests that don't lead to a booking are deleted within 24 months. Booking records are kept for as long as tax and accounting law requires.

You can ask to see, correct or delete your data, or object to how we use it, by emailing us. If you are in Georgia, the Law of Georgia on Personal Data Protection applies; if you are in the EU/EEA or UK, you also have rights under the GDPR, including the right to complain to your local data protection authority.
Booking terms for Million First Steps journeys.
The small print, in plain words

These terms are being finalised before we accept our first bookings. Until then, the written quote we send you sets out the conditions for your trip — nothing is binding until you have read it and confirmed.

Prices on this website are “from” prices per person, based on two travellers sharing, and are for guidance. Your exact price depends on dates, party size and availability, and is confirmed in writing in your personal quote.
Your journey is confirmed when you accept your quote and we receive the deposit stated in it. The balance is due by the date in your quote, usually a few weeks before arrival.

Want to change something? Tell us as early as possible and we'll do our best — some changes may affect the price. If you need to cancel, the charges depend on how close to departure you cancel and on what we have already paid to hotels and partners; the exact scale is set out in your quote.
If we ever have to change a significant part of your trip, we'll offer an equivalent alternative or a refund for the affected part.
Comprehensive travel insurance, including medical cover and cancellation, is required for every traveller.

Some journeys include mountain roads and hikes at altitude. Please tell us about any health or mobility needs so we can plan safely. Your guide may adapt a route for weather or safety — their decision is final.
If something isn't right during your trip, tell your guide or call us straight away so we can fix it while you're here. After your trip, write to us at hello@millionfirststeps.ge.
These terms are governed by the laws of Georgia. This does not remove any rights you may have under the consumer laws of your own country.
